orders.description: Defendants' limited appeal from the October 4, 2012 order denying the complaint-dismissal branch of their motion.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied the branch of defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff slipped on liquid on the floor of Hannaford's supermarket on July 9, 2007. The liquid covered an approximately four-by-one-foot area near a cart holding items to be re-shelved.

legal_issues.finding: Noncreation is stated as part of the initial burden; the application rests on constructive notice without separately deciding creation.
Actual notice appears in the initial-burden rule; no separate actual-notice finding is made.
Defendants failed to eliminate a triable issue of constructive notice; the court did not conclusively find notice or negligence.

quality.notes: Private retail control is supported by express supermarket operation; ownership is not inferred. Other hazard means liquid of unspecified composition, not necessarily water. Proximity to the re-shop cart does not establish that it created the spill. The source identifies no specific evidence types or plaintiff role. The appeal fully affirms the appealed branch; the accident predates the opinion and its explicit 2007 date is preserved.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs.

On July 9, 2007, the plaintiff slipped and fell on liquid on the floor of a supermarket operated by the defendant Hannaford Bros. Co. The area covered by liquid measured approximately four feet by one foot, and was located in the vicinity of the “re-shop cart” into which were placed items to be re-shelved.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendants appeal, as limited by their brief, from so much of an order of the Supreme Court, Dutchess County (Forman, J.), dated October 4, 2012, as denied that branch of their motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

“A defendant moving for summary judgment in a slip-and-fall case has the initial burden of making a prima facie showing that it neither created the hazardous condition nor had actual or constructive notice of its existence for a sufficient length of time to discover and remedy it”
Here, the defendants failed to meet that burden since they did not demonstrate the absence of a triable issue of fact as to whether they had constructive notice of the allegedly hazardous condition

Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied that branch of the defendants’ motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, regardless of the sufficiency of the plaintiff’s opposition papers

orders.description: Executrix's appeal from the May 31, 2013 order denying her summary-judgment motion.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly tripped on a loose or dislodged slate tile on an exterior step abutting premises owned by defendant's decedent.

legal_issues.finding: The court stated noncreation as part of the threshold burden; its application does not separately decide creation.
Defendant failed to establish absence of actual notice by her decedent; the court did not conclusively find notice.
Defendant failed to establish absence of constructive notice by her decedent; the threshold burden remained on defendant.
The court clarified that defendant must first establish lack of notice before the sufficiency of plaintiff's opposition becomes relevant.
Defendant also failed to establish that the alleged slate condition was neither defective nor dangerous as a matter of law.

evidence_discussed.description: The court refers to defendant's submissions on dangerousness without identifying their form; no specific testimony, photographs or reports are inferred.

quality.notes: Property review concerns the actual exterior step: the text establishes ownership of abutting premises, but not explicitly ownership/control/private status of the step. Do not infer public ownership either. Owner role refers to the decedent's abutting premises; other refers to the executrix, not personal ownership. Premises subtype, plaintiff role and accident date are unstated. Obstruction denotes the alleged loose tile, not a final finding of danger.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, without costs or disbursements.
The plaintiff alleges that she tripped and fell over a dislodged or loose piece of slate tile on an exterior step abutting premises owned by the defendant's decedent.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendant appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (Garguilo, J.), dated May 31, 2013, which denied her motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

To demonstrate prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law in a premises liability case, a defendant owner must establish that it did not create the condition that allegedly caused the fall or have actual or constructive notice of that condition

On a defendant's motion for summary judgment, it is not the plaintiff's burden in opposing the motion to establish that the defendants had actual or constructive notice of the hazardous condition; rather, it is the defendant's burden to establish the lack of notice as a matter of law
Here, the defendant failed to establish, as a matter of law, that her decedent had neither actual nor constructive notice of the allegedly defective condition

Furthermore, contrary to the defendant's alternate contention, the defendant's submissions on the motion failed to establish that the condition complained of was neither defective nor dangerous as a matter of law
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Carol A. Hecht, Respondent, v Kim P. Saccoccio, as Executrix of Rosemarie A. Colonna, Deceased, Appellant.

orders.description: Plaintiff's appeal from the March 14, 2016 order limited to the dismissal of the complaint against Rob-Lee Corp.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted the motion branch seeking summary judgment dismissing the complaint against Rob-Lee Corp.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly tripped while descending an interior staircase in Rob-Lee's building on November 28, 2012. One side had a metal handrail; the other had a partial wall topped by a wooden guardrail, and plaintiff testified she found nothing to grasp on that side.

legal_issues.finding: The court recognized an undisputed requirement for a second handrail; whether the partial wall satisfied the applicable requirement remained disputed.
Plaintiff's inability to grasp the partial wall and conflicting compliance evidence raised a triable issue of causal connection; causation was not conclusively found.

Although a second handrail was required, conflicting evidence raised factual questions whether the partial wall complied with Building Code section 765.4(a)(11) and whether any violation caused injury.
Plaintiff submitted an engineering affidavit asserting Building Code violations and raised a triable issue in opposition to defendants' prima facie no-defect showing.

evidence_discussed.description: Defendants submitted parties' deposition testimony; plaintiff testified she found nothing to grasp at the partial wall.
Photographs supported defendants' prima facie no-defect showing, which plaintiff's opposition successfully put in dispute.
Plaintiff's engineering affidavit alleged violations of the 1984 Building Code relevant to the second handrail.

quality.notes: Defendants met their initial burden but plaintiff raised a triable issue; this is not described as an initial defense failure or a proven code violation. Full reversal of the appealed Rob-Lee branch is binary 1, not mixed; other defendants' claims are outside the appealed scope. Owner refers to Rob-Lee only; roles of other named defendants are unstated. Building use and plaintiff's role are not inferred from party names.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed insofar as appealed from, on the law, with costs, and that branch of the motion of the defendants Rob-Lee Corp., Bill Elliot, and William E. Rosenblatt which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant Rob-Lee Corp. is denied.
On November 28, 2012, the plaintiff allegedly was injured when she tripped and fell while descending an interior staircase located in a building owned by the defendant Rob-Lee Corp.

The order, insofar as appealed from, granted that branch of the motion of the defendants Rob-Lee Corp., Bill Elliot, and William E. Rosenblatt which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant Rob-Lee Corp.

On one side of the staircase, there was a wall and a metal handrail attached to the wall. On the other side of the staircase, there was a partial wall with a wooden guardrail on top and open space above the partial wall.

The defendants established their prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against Rob-Lee Corp. by submitting, inter alia, the deposition testimony of the parties and photographs, which demonstrated that there was no defective condition on the stairway

In opposition, the plaintiff argued, inter alia, that the absence of a second handrail proximately caused her injuries. She submitted the affidavit of an engineering expert, who averred that the condition of the staircase violated various provisions of the 1984 New York State Fire Prevention and Building Code (hereinafter the Building Code).
The plaintiff raised a triable issue of fact regarding the absence of a second handrail.
There is no dispute that the staircase required a second handrail

Given the plaintiff's deposition testimony that there was nothing to grasp when she reached for the partial wall to her left, coupled with conflicting evidence as to whether the partial wall complied with section 765.4 (a) (11) of the Building Code, triable issues of fact exist as to whether the Building Code was violated and whether a violation of that section of the Building Code, if any, was a proximate cause of the plaintiff's injuries
Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have denied that branch of the defendants' motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against Rob-Lee Corp.

orders.description: Plaintiff's appeal from the June 2, 2021 order granting defendants summary judgment and dismissing the complaint.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendants' summary-judgment motion and dismissed the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff slipped on a clear liquid in a Dollar General aisle on premises owned by 9274 Group and leased to Dolgencorp. The assistant manager said she walked that aisle about 15 minutes earlier and saw nothing on the floor.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants asserted noncreation in their underlying motion; it was not disputed or separately analyzed on appeal.
Defendants asserted lack of actual notice in their underlying motion; the only disputed appellate issue was constructive notice.

The manager's specific inspection account established lack of constructive notice. Video that did not capture the accident area neither confirmed nor contradicted that account and raised no triable issue.

evidence_discussed.description: Assistant manager's affidavit supplied a specific inspection account, generally consistent with her deposition.

Plaintiff relied on store footage to challenge inspection timing. The court found it omitted the fall area and neither confirmed nor refuted the manager; no independent footage review was performed here.

quality.notes: Clear liquid is not necessarily water; other hazard preserves unknown composition. Specific owner/tenant roles are explicit. The footage is neutral as to the claimed inspection, not affirmative proof that it occurred. Actual notice and creation remain underlying motion contentions rather than invented appellate findings. Accident date and plaintiff's role are unstated.

evidence.quote: It is hereby ordered that the order so appealed from is unanimously affirmed without costs.

Memorandum: Plaintiff commenced this action seeking damages for injuries she sustained when she slipped and fell on a clear liquid while walking down an aisle in a Dollar General Store owned by defendant 9274 Group, Inc., which leased the premises to defendant Dolgencorp of New York, Inc.
The order granted the motion of defendants for summary judgment and dismissed the complaint.

Following discovery, defendants moved for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, contending, inter alia, that they did not create the dangerous condition that caused plaintiff's accident and lacked actual or constructive notice of it.
The only disputed issue on appeal is whether defendants had constructive notice of the dangerous condition in the store.

Here, defendants met their initial burden of establishing the lack of constructive notice as a matter of law through the affidavit of the assistant store manager, who stated that she inspected the premises every 30 minutes to check for safety hazards, and that she walked down the aisle in question approximately 15 minutes before plaintiff fell and did not see anything on the floor.
The assistant manager offered deposition testimony that is generally consistent with her affidavit.

In opposition to the motion, plaintiff relied largely on footage from surveillance cameras inside the store that, according to plaintiff, call into question the assistant manager's assertions that she inspected the area 15 minutes before the accident.

Based on our review of the relevant footage, which does not capture the area where plaintiff fell, we conclude that it neither confirms nor refutes the sworn assertions of the assistant manager with respect to her inspection of that area, and that the court therefore properly concluded that plaintiff failed to raise an issue of fact sufficient to defeat defendants' motion for summary judgment.
We affirm.

orders.description: Gap's appeal from the March 31, 2021 order adhering upon renewal to its earlier denial of summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted renewal but adhered to the June 5, 2020 denial of Gap's motion to dismiss the complaint against it.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff alleged that she stepped backwards and slipped on a security tag on the floor of Gap's Queens store on May 15, 2018. The submitted surveillance footage was described as contradicting that account and showing a trip over her own feet.

legal_issues.finding: Defendant's evidence established a trip over plaintiff's own feet rather than a security-tag slip; her contrary account was contradicted by the footage and raised no triable issue.
The submitted deposition and footage established prima facie that no dangerous or defective floor condition existed; plaintiff failed to raise a factual issue.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff's deposition asserted a backward step and security-tag slip; the court found it contradicted by the footage.
Defendant submitted accident footage establishing a trip over plaintiff's own feet and contradicting the alleged tag mechanism. Only the supplied opinion, not the video itself, was read.

quality.notes: One independently appealed order: March 31, 2021. Vacatur of the prior June 5, 2020 order is consequential relief upon renewal, not a second appeal or mixed outcome. This is substantive negligence review after renewal, not a procedural-only renewal dispute. Fall type slip_or_trip preserves alleged slip and supported trip; either is within incident scope. Obstruction records the alleged security tag only, not an established hazard. A failed negligence claim remains eligible. Plaintiff's customer/visitor status is unstated.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order dated March 31, 2021, is reversed insofar as appealed from, on the law, with costs, upon renewal, the order dated June 5, 2020, is vacated, and the motion of the defendant Gap, Inc., for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it is granted.
On May 15, 2018, the plaintiff allegedly was injured when she slipped and fell over a security tag on the floor of a store in Queens owned by the defendant Gap, Inc. (hereinafter the defendant).

The order, insofar as appealed from, upon renewal, adhered to the determination in an order of the same court dated June 5, 2020, denying that defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it.

The defendant established its prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it through the submission of, inter alia, a transcript of the plaintiff's deposition testimony and video surveillance footage of the accident.
This evidence established, prima facie, that no dangerous or defective condition existed on the floor of the store and that the plaintiff tripped over her own feet
Contrary to the plaintiff's contention, her deposition testimony that she stepped backwards and slipped on a security tag is belied by the video surveillance footage
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact.
Accordingly, upon renewal, the Supreme Court should have granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it.
